claims.text: The initial zirconium-alloy cladding has a pure elemental Cr coating deposited by conventional physical vapor deposition.
Adding 2–5 wt.% Al to the Cr coating will improve coating durability.
Al addition will promote formation of Al2O3 at or near the Cr–Zr interface.
The resulting Al2O3 layer will be stable and adherent during high-temperature exposure.
Al in the Cr–Al coating oxidizes preferentially at elevated temperatures to form alumina.
The Al2O3 layer acts as a barrier to oxidant ingress.
The Al2O3 layer limits diffusion of Cr into Zr and Zr into Cr.
The Cr–Al coating will have better oxidation resistance than a pure Cr coating.
Under approximately 300°C water exposure for up to 1000 hours, the modified coating will retain its protective attributes without significant degradation.
Under approximately 1200°C steam exposure for 1–2 hours, the Cr–Al coating will maintain better integrity than the pure Cr baseline.
The Cr–Al coating will reduce interfacial Cr–Zr interdiffusion relative to the pure Cr baseline.
The Cr–Al coating will provide improved performance relative to pure Cr under both subcritical-water and accident-relevant steam regimes.
Elevated-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion in the pure Cr baseline leads to premature coating failure under accident conditions.
The proposed intervention is applicable up to approximately 1200°C in steam for 1–2 hours and approximately 300°C in water for about 1000 hours.
The optimal Al concentration and deposition parameters for producing a uniform, stable alumina barrier without degrading initial coating properties are not established.
Long-term cyclic exposure or radiation may affect the stability of the Cr–Al coating.
